summary:
Santa Cruz stands under Argentina's national framework on gender identity, and no provincial departure from that framework material enough to score separately has been sourced. The executive decrees of 5 February 2025 that narrowed the national framework apply to every province, Santa Cruz included. The operating position for a visitor to the province is the national one.

Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, and an 'X' marker has been available on the national identity document since 2021. The United Nations described the statute as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Trans activists interviewed in April 2025 report that the law remains formally in force but is no longer guaranteed in practice.

DNU 62/2025 amended Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law to bar under-18s from gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions; international press reported the resulting ban on surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents. Legal experts and LGBTIQ+ organisations call the decree unconstitutional and warn that abruptly suspending adolescent treatment endangers trans youth. The decree faces judicial challenge, and the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

DNU 61/2025 altered the sentencing framework so as to change where trans detainees are held. It is challenged on the same grounds as the decree on minors and its status is likewise unresolved in the sources available here.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a record, averaging one every 38 hours; the figures were reported on 19 March 2026 and described as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, who was stabbed to death. The Court rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, which an appeal court had removed in 2020, with the result that the gender-motivated-crime aggravator does not apply in the case as it now stands.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial instruments. An international LGBTIQ+ rights organisation's country overview, updated on 12 March 2026, nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed on 4 April 2025 told an international publication that the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate. Among those interviewed were figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins.
localsOnly:
The national ministry responsible for women, gender and diversity was eliminated under President Javier Milei, and trans hires made under the federal Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserves 1% of public-sector posts, were dismissed; activists say the quota is no longer being implemented.

Residents under 18 face the suspension of gender-affirming surgical and hormonal treatment under DNU 62/2025, and legal experts and LGBTIQ+ organisations petitioned the courts to intervene, describing the suspension as dangerous to trans youth. No source available here records how the decree is being applied by health providers in Santa Cruz.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the judicial challenge to DNU 62/2025 and DNU 61/2025 is unresolved in the sources available here; neither their validity nor their final scope of application is recorded.

No source available here addresses entry or visa rules for trans visitors, border or airport screening that risks involuntary disclosure, restroom or facility access in Santa Cruz, or provincial-level partner recognition beyond the national framework.

Whether the national 'X' document marker continues to be issued in practice after the February 2025 decrees is unresolved in these sources. Provincial enforcement of the hate-crime recording machinery and of the Trans Labor Quota Law within Santa Cruz is likewise not sourced.
